analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products and restrict youth smoking.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health committee on May 16, 2000 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written tobacco products into the federal food and drug law for the first time, giving the Secretary of Health and Human Services and the FDA power to regulate them. It required companies to disclose every ingredient and nicotine delivery data, let the FDA restrict youth access and advertising, set performance standards for cigarettes, recall defective products, and review new tobacco products before they could be sold. It also carved tobacco growers out of FDA authority and left the power to ban cigarettes outright with Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially children, by reducing youth access to tobacco and marketing aimed at them; the bill's own findings estimated that cutting youth smoking by half would prevent well over 60,000 early deaths a year and save up to $43 billion annually in medical costs and lost productivity. Health agencies would gain enforcement tools they lacked after courts struck down the FDA's 1996 attempt to regulate tobacco.

how_it_helps.text: Grants the Secretary of Health and Human Services explicit regulatory authority over tobacco products under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, including standards for adulteration, misbranding, and manufacturing practices.
Requires manufacturers to disclose all ingredients, nicotine content and delivery, and their internal research on health and marketing effects, on an ongoing basis.

Lets the FDA restrict access to and advertising of tobacco products whenever needed to prevent or reduce use by children, and bars FDA staff from tobacco farms only for growers not controlled by manufacturers.
Gives the FDA authority to order cessation of distribution and recall of a tobacco product found to have a defect likely to cause serious health consequences or death.
Requires premarket review of new tobacco products and creates a defined pathway for 'reduced risk' products, so new products must show they pose no greater public health risk before sale.
The bill's findings estimate that reducing tobacco use by minors by 50 percent would prevent well over 60,000 early deaths each year and save up to $43 billion annually.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the compliance costs: registration, biennial inspections, ingredient and nicotine disclosure, premarket applications, recall exposure, and advertising limits. Retail outlets selling tobacco face advertising restrictions if minors can enter. Tobacco leaf growers are explicitly exempted, so they pay nothing.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local rules on performance standards, labeling, registration, and reduced-risk products, so states could keep stricter rules only on sale, distribution, and access, not on product standards.
Tobacco leaf growers, warehouses, and cooperatives are exempted from FDA authority, and FDA employees may not enter a grower's farm without written consent.

The bill expressly reserves to Congress any decision to eliminate all cigarettes or smokeless tobacco or cut nicotine to zero, so the regulator could never take those steps, and the Secretary may not require prior approval of advertisement content.

Compliance would impose real costs on manufacturers, and the bill directs the FDA to account for manufacturers' financial resources when setting effective dates for manufacturing standards, which could delay protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains were potentially very large under the bill's own estimates, while the costs fall mainly on a single industry that profited from an unregulated product. The bill's main weaknesses are its carve-outs: growers are exempt, states lose some of their stricter authority, and the deepest options like a product ban or zero-nicotine requirement were reserved to Congress. Even with those limits, it was a substantial expansion of oversight over a product the bill's own findings call a 'pediatric disease of epic proportions.'

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Frist (R-TN), joined by Sen. John McCain, introduced the bill on May 16, 2000.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is listed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, who faced no new federal regulatory regime; FDA authority over tobacco did not arrive until the 2009 Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act. Tobacco growers also stayed outside any FDA oversight.

sides.party_line_note: The only senators on record are Republicans (Frist as sponsor, one Republican cosponsor), and no vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured; the bill was introduced in an election year after earlier bipartisan tobacco efforts had failed.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, ingredient and nicotine disclosure, premarket review, recall exposure, and advertising restrictions on cigarette makers — but it also entrenched their product's legal status: Congress reserved to itself any ban, states lost some stricter authority, and 'reduced risk' products got a defined marketing pathway. Tobacco companies had long fought FDA authority in court and in Congress, so their interest ran against the bill's public health purpose.
The bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf producers from FDA authority and bars FDA staff from entering farms without written consent, so growers escape regulation entirely under this framework.

Retail outlets accessible to minors would face advertising restrictions under regulations the Secretary must issue, though the bill bars any prohibition on face-to-face sales by a category of retail outlets.

industries.industry: Health agencies and public health community
industries.note: HHS and the FDA would gain explicit statutory authority, inspection and recall powers, and mandatory industry data submissions, tools the bill says federal and state officials lacked.
